Opening: Ferber tells Bill he feels sorry for Elaine; Hartigan points out to Elaine which woman is Elaine, which is Hartigan herself, and which is Jane Freilicher; art students see in them proof that de Kooning is homosexual, relying on what look like bullet holes — in fact very chic “rubies” stuck on the skin, seen in Harper's Bazaar; violently negative reviews (Time: “mighty ugly … mid-20th-century dames”).
Willem de Kooning's first solo exhibition at Sidney Janis's
Paintings on the Theme of the Woman opened on March 16 with six Woman paintings and sixteen drawings and pastels on the theme. Only two works sold; Mrs. John D. Rockefeller III bought Woman II.

He asks de Kooning for a drawing to erase and present as his own work; de Kooning gives him a drawing in pencil, crayon, and perhaps ink, hard to erase. He spends nearly a month erasing it; traces of the original marks remain.
Morrissette is said to have told Robbe-Grillet about the Erased de Kooning Drawing

Robbe-Grillet's first American advocate is said to have told the author of Les Gommes (1953) early on about the other erasure of that year: Rauschenberg's Erased de Kooning Drawing, seeing a “chosiste” convergence between the two men.

Rauschenberg laboriously erases a drawing that de Kooning had given him for the purpose, having chosen a drawing that was hard to erase; de Kooning does not entirely appreciate the publicity surrounding the event.
Joint Rauschenberg/Twombly exhibition at the Stable Gallery and Cage's manifesto

A joint exhibition of Rauschenberg (paintings and sculptures, including the two- and seven-panel White Paintings) and Twombly; the public mostly baffled. A few weeks later, Cage publishes in Emily Genauer's column in the New York Herald Tribune his first manifesto on Rauschenberg, “no subject / no image / no taste…,” a pastiche of the style of Breton and Aragon transposed into Zen-Dada.
